chapter: Ella, Charlie Christian and Europe with Hayes
title: Mr. Kramer and daughter Ethel: early confusion about prejudice
summary: At 12 he was confused by a German blacksmith neighbour, Mr. Kramer, and his daughter Ethel, who treated him with kindness unlike others around him.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: I'm surprised that you put two and two together so early, at the age of 24.
Because you hadn't even -- by that time you were only still exploring your own --
Well, at 12 I had put two and two together.

Yeah. Because there was a German blacksmith when I was in Pittsburgh, and I was going to school with his daughter, and he was such a fantastic blacksmith that everyone would come and bring their horse to him. Even my grandfather had two mules, and everyone would -- Mr. Kramer, his name was. And his daughter and I became staunch friends, and we used to go to school arm in arm, you know, and he would always just pat me and say, 'Good boy, Kenny.' And I said to myself, I said, 'Why is this man so nice and every place else I go people are just the opposite?' You know?
And that kind of confused me, you know?

And her name -- what was her name? Ethel Kramer. And she was a sweet little girl, very smart, and we finished school together, and then I started playing music and the family moved away, you know, after automobiles came, and
Mr. Kramer just gave it up.
But I always -- often think of her, that sweet girl.
Yeah, because that was just a natural thing.
It was a natural thing for her. I was a kid, she was a kid, and we went to school together. We had the same interests, you know.
And her father never taught her anything but to be nice, you know, and be careful and be nice, that's all.
Not to teach contempt and -- no, I know he never --
No, because he was too great a person to do that. And when I think back, I say Mr. Kramer could never be mean. He just wasn't that type of man, you jknow.
And I wanted to go away. At 12.
Yeah. In other words, you had sensitivities, and they were hurt early on.
I mean some people manage to block it out or they figure it has to be lived with.
And they don't accept the message or whatever.
No, but Mr. Kramer was -- he was just a man, a good man, you know, a good God fearing man. He just believed in humanity.

Because all of his customers were people like my grandfather, and he always frequented the families and had his business in our neighborhood, so he became attached to the people in the neighborhood, which is only normal.
After thinking about it, you know -- I often think of Mr, Kramer, even now I think about him.
It shows you what -- you never know in life what just being right, what effect it has on other
Well, she was -- Ethel was like a buddy, you know.
You know, I always looked at her like a buddy. We were kids, and she was always a buddy, you know.

She would say, 'Kenny, you hungry? Come on in and have some tea,' or something like that. And Mr. Kramer would come in for lunch and we'd be having tea, and, 'How are you son?' So and so, how's school, and things like that, and that was it.
And I had never seen people like that, when I was a kid.
Everyone was so hostile and, I don't know. It just kind of turned me off. I wanted to go away, you know.
It's hard enough to make it in life without having to contend with animosities.
Well, did you -- did you talk to guys, or did you just keep your own counsel?
